content: 1. Adults with an APRI score of ≤2, persistently normal ALT levels, and low levels of HBV DNA replication (<2000 IU/mL) may defer treatment, regardless of HBeAg status or age. This is a strong recommendation, though based on low-quality evidence. 2. In settings where HBV DNA testing is unavailable, treatment can be deferred in HBeAg-positive individuals aged 30 years or younger with persistently normal ALT levels. This is a conditional recommendation with low-quality evidence. 3. Regular monitoring is essential for all individuals with chronic hepatitis B (CHB), especially those who do not currently meet treatment criteria, to assess if antiviral therapy may be needed in the future to prevent progressive liver disease. 4. For adults, adolescents, and children aged 12 years or older who require antiviral therapy, nucleos(t)ide analogues (NAs) with a high barrier to drug resistance, such as tenofovir or entecavir, are recommended. Entecavir is specifically recommended for children aged 2–11 years. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 5. NAs with a low barrier to resistance, such as lamivudine, adefovir, or telbivudine, are not recommended due to the risk of drug resistance. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 6. For individuals co-infected with HBV and HIV, a fixed-dose combination of tenofovir, lamivudine (or emtricitabine), and efavirenz is the preferred first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART). This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 7. Individuals with cirrhosis, based on clinical evidence or an APRI score >2, require lifelong treatment with NAs and should not discontinue antiviral therapy due to the risk of reactivation, which can lead to severe acute-on-chronic liver injury. This is a strong recommendation with low-quality evidence. 8. Discontinuation of NA therapy may be considered in exceptional cases for individuals without cirrhosis (APRI score ≤2), who can be carefully monitored long-term for reactivation, and who demonstrate HBeAg loss and seroconversion to anti-HBe (if initially HBeAg-positive) after at least one additional year of treatment. Persistent normal ALT levels and undetectable HBV DNA levels are also required. In settings without HBV DNA testing, discontinuation may be considered in individuals with persistent HBsAg loss after at least one additional year of treatment, regardless of prior HBeAg status. This is a conditional recommendation with low-quality evidence. 9. Relapse may occur after stopping NA therapy, necessitating careful monitoring for disease progression and treatment response before, during, and after treatment. 10. Annual monitoring is recommended for ALT levels (and AST for APRI), HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV DNA levels (if available). Non-invasive tests, such as APRI or FibroScan, should be used to assess for cirrhosis in those without baseline cirrhosis. Adherence to treatment should be regularly monitored at each visit. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 11. More frequent monitoring may be required for individuals with intermittently abnormal ALT levels or fluctuating HBV DNA levels between 2000 IU/mL and 20,000 IU/mL (if HBV DNA testing is available), as well as for those co-infected with HIV. This is a conditional recommendation with low-quality evidence. 12. For individuals on treatment or following treatment discontinuation, more frequent monitoring (at least every 3 months during the first year) is recommended for those with advanced liver disease (compensated or decompensated cirrhosis), during the first year of treatment to assess response and adherence, in cases where adherence is a concern, in HIV co-infected individuals, and after treatment discontinuation. 13. Baseline renal function and risk factors for renal dysfunction should be assessed before initiating antiviral therapy. Renal function should be monitored annually in individuals on long-term tenofovir or entecavir therapy, and growth should be carefully monitored in children. 14. All infants should receive their first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, preferably within 24 hours, followed by two or three additional doses. 15. In HBV-monoinfected pregnant women, treatment indications are the same as for other adults, and tenofovir is recommended. However, no recommendation is made for the routine use of antiviral therapy to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HBV. 16. In HIV-infected pregnant and breastfeeding women, a once-daily fixed-dose combination of tenofovir, lamivudine (or emtricitabine), and efavirenz is recommended as first-line ART. This applies to both lifelong treatment and ART initiated for prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) and then stopped. This is a strong recommendation with low-to-moderate quality evidence. 17. Lifelong NA therapy is required for individuals with cirrhosis, as discontinuation poses a high risk of reactivation and severe liver injury. 18. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of monitoring for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in individuals with cirrhosis or a family history of HCC, as well as regular monitoring for disease progression and treatment response in all individuals with CHB. 19. The guidelines are designed to support policymakers in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) in developing national hepatitis B prevention and treatment plans, as well as to assist clinicians managing individuals with CHB. 20. The overarching goal of the WHO is to achieve the highest possible level of health for all people, with a focus on incorporating human rights principles, including confidentiality and informed decision-making, into hepatitis B care and treatment policies.
